analysis.one_liner: Caps malpractice payouts, restricts lawsuits over medical injuries, and shields free emergency care from liability.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, never received a committee vote, and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the rules for lawsuits over medical injuries nationwide. It capped pain-and-suffering awards at $250,000 per doctor and $500,000 total from all institutions, capped total wrongful-death recovery from any single doctor at $1.4 million, shortened filing deadlines, required expert reports within 120 days or dismissal, and made each defendant pay only its own proportionate share. It also shielded health providers who give free emergency care from liability except for willful or wanton misconduct.
analysis.who_benefits: Physicians, hospitals, nursing homes, and the insurers that cover them gain the most: damage caps and the $1.4 million total cap in wrongful-death cases directly reduce their worst-case payouts and malpractice insurance exposure. Periodic payment of large future awards and proportionate liability further limit what any single defendant pays. The limits apply regardless of how egregious the error was.

how_it_helps.text: Caps non-economic (pain and suffering) damages at $250,000 against all liable health care practitioners combined and $250,000 per institution, $500,000 from all liable institutions combined, no matter how many are at fault [S2][S3].
Caps total damages of every kind — including compensatory and punitive — at $1.4 million (inflation-adjusted) from any single doctor in a wrongful-death case [S2][S3].
Lets defendants with $100,000 or more in future damages pay them out over time instead of up front, and makes each defendant pay only its proportionate share of fault [S2][S3].
Grants immunity to health care practitioners and institutions that provide free emergency 'Good Samaritan' care, except for willful or wanton negligence [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients seriously harmed by medical negligence — and families of those killed — bear the cost. Someone with enormous pain, suffering, or loss of companionship but modest lost wages (a child, a retiree, a stay-at-home parent) would see their recovery slashed to the caps, and a two-year deadline with no extension for children over 12 would bar some valid claims entirely. The savings to doctors and insurers are not tied to any requirement that they lower prices or pass anything on to patients.

drawbacks.text: The caps fall hardest on people whose main loss is pain and suffering rather than wages — children, retirees, and stay-at-home parents — and nothing in the bill requires insurers or providers to pass savings to patients through lower prices or premiums [S2][S3].

Claims must generally be filed within two years, cannot be tolled for minors' status after age 12, and face an absolute 10-year repose with no tolling for any reason — deadlines that would extinguish injuries discovered late, such as slowly developing harm or a foreign object left in a body [S3].

A plaintiff who rejects a defense settlement offer and wins less than 80% of it at trial must pay the defense's litigation costs, including attorney fees and expert fees — a risk that could pressure families into settling cheap cases involving legitimate injuries [S3].

The honest trade-off supporters must acknowledge: malpractice suits do impose real costs on doctors through premiums and defensive medicine, but this bill buys any reduction in those costs entirely with the compensation owed to the most severely injured patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is lopsided: every provision reduces what negligent providers and their insurers pay, while the benefit to the public — cheaper malpractice insurance and less defensive medicine — is indirect, unproven by anything in the bill itself, and not linked to any price or premium reduction. Meanwhile it shortens deadlines, shifts fee risk onto plaintiffs, and immunizes free emergency care. On its face it is a transfer of loss from the health care industry to injured patients.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, no other member signed on, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Burgess (R-TX) introduced the Medical Justice Act of 2007 on September 10, 2007 [S1][S2].

It was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary, which never considered it; the only further action was the sponsor's introductory remarks printed in the Congressional Record on October 2, 2007 [S5].
No member of either party cosponsored the bill [S4].
The 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill died without a hearing, a markup, or a vote in any chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients injured by medical negligence and their families keep full access to the courts and uncapped compensation for non-economic harm, and plaintiffs' trial lawyers keep the existing liability system. Doctors, hospitals, and malpractice insurers do not get the caps they sought — though with zero cosponsors the bill never had traction, so the industry lost little it realistically expected to win.

for.name: Rep. Michael C. Burgess
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medical Justice Act of 2007 and delivered introductory remarks on it [S1][S5].

against.name: Rep. John Conyers
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, keeping it from any floor consideration [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's Republican sponsor drew zero cosponsors from either party in a Democratic-controlled House [S4].

industries.note: Caps on non-economic and total damages, proportionate liability, and mandatory periodic payments directly reduce the maximum payouts insurers must cover. Insurers pay nothing for this benefit, and nothing in the bill requires premium reductions for policyholders. Sources: [S2][S3]

The $250,000 pain-and-suffering cap and $1.4 million wrongful-death cap slash worst-case exposure, and the expert-report rules require plaintiffs to clear procedural hurdles within 120 days or have claims dismissed with attorney fees awarded to the doctor. Sources: [S2][S3]

industries.industry: Hospitals, nursing homes, and other care institutions
industries.note: Institutions face a $250,000 cap each and $500,000 total from all liable institutions, and gain Good Samaritan immunity for free emergency care. Nursing homes and hospices are explicitly covered as 'health care institutions.' Sources: [S2][S3]

Damage caps shrink contingent fees, and the defense-initiated settlement process plus 120-day expert-report requirement shift fee and cost risk onto plaintiffs' counsel. Their financial interest here runs alongside their clients' access to full recovery. Sources: [S2][S3]
